newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Dalgety pledges to turn around.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Dalgety pledges to turn around.

text.p: British petfoods and agricultural company Dalgety Plc is determined to turn itself around after a dreadful fourth quarter's trading and its second profit warning in two months, chief executive Richard Clothier said in an interview on Tuesday.
"I believe that as a result of this announcement we can look forward to a substantial improvement this year and next," said Clothier.
"I am very encouraged by the tough thinking and hard line taken by our finance director."

Kenneth Hanna took over from John Martyn as finance director on May 1. Hanna has taken a more prudent approach to accounting for bad debt provisions, insurance claims and the value put on assets, Clothier said.
"We have got to turn around the petfoods business. We have got to concentrate on fixing it. We have not got our costs down fast enough."

Earlier, the company announced an increase in petfoods' exceptional costs to 67 million stg from 30 million envisaged in its previous profits warning in May. It made additional provisions for surplus property of 15 million and an accounting adjustment for goodwill of up to 50 million to be made in the 1997 accounts.

Total exceptional charges will amount to 138 million compared to 36 million indicated in May. The company said its profits for the year ended June 30 would be lower than expected, not less than 65 million before tax, sending its shares 40 pence lower to 221-1/2p pence in early trade.

Hugh Donaldson, who took over from Nigel Garrow as chief executive of Petfoods two months ago, has identified more areas where costs can be saved, Clothier said. This will involve job losses and plant closures but Clothier said he could not yet give details.

Once changes at the group's petfoods division have been completed, they will give rise to savings of some 20 million stg per annum, with 8.0 million coming through in 1997/98 and 12 million the year after, said Clothier.
In May the group calculated a shake-up in its petfoods division would bring a benefit of 12 million stg. Dalgety owns the Felix petfood brand.

On trading, Clothier said a dry spring period meant cattle grazed for longer and reduced the need for animal feed. June, which is an important month for fertiliser sales by Dalgety, was exceptionally wet which prevented farmers from getting into fields to fertilise or to spray pesticide onto their crops.
